title: The French Inside Your English
subtitle: The register ladder, the word for 'it', and your first sentences

use_example.german: Je le veux, un peu.
use_example.english: I want it, a little.

summary.takeaway: The formal register of English is a French warehouse — and the word for 'it' is the word for 'the', walking one step left.

title: Hidden Twins: Places & Colors
subtitle: Recognition gym: words that crossed the Channel and stayed themselves

use_example.german: La maison est grande et l'hôtel est petit.
use_example.english: The house is big and the hotel is small.

summary.takeaway: When a word needs no rule, recognition is the whole skill — your eye first, then your mouth.

title: First Sentences Gym
subtitle: Je veux… pattern drills with everything from lesson 1

use_example.german: Tu la veux ? — Oui, un peu.
use_example.english: Do you want it? — Yes, a little.

summary.takeaway: Check the noun's article, then let the pronoun walk: the check-then-move habit is the whole pronoun system in embryo.

title: The Register Ladder
subtitle: Climb from everyday Germanic English to formal Latinate English and find French waiting

use_example.german: Je veux entrer et continuer.
use_example.english: I want to go in and keep going.

summary.takeaway: When a two-word English verb blocks you, step up to its one-word formal synonym — that word is already French.

title: The -ION Bridge
subtitle: Thousands of nouns convert whole — and every one is feminine

use_example.german: Je veux la confirmation. — Je la veux.
use_example.english: I want the confirmation. — I want it.

summary.takeaway: -ION is a gender decoder: the ending is feminine, the article is la, and 'it' is that same la, walking.

title: L'Elision Gym
subtitle: The apostrophe marks a vowel sacrificed — la → l', le → l'

use_example.german: L'opinion est intéressante.
use_example.english: The opinion is interesting.

summary.takeaway: The apostrophe is a vowel's tombstone: la opinion → l'opinion, but the walking pronoun never elides.

title: -ION Discrimination Drills
subtitle: la or l' — decide at speed, then build the pronoun

use_example.german: Merci pour l'invitation — j'accepte la complication.
use_example.english: Thanks for the invitation — I accept the complication.

summary.takeaway: Two glances per noun: -ION → feminine; vowel → elide. The rule is in the word, not in a list.

title: The -ation Engine
subtitle: Noun → verb: confirmation → confirmer. Thousands of infinitives, almost free

use_example.german: Je veux réserver une table.
use_example.english: I want to reserve a table.

summary.takeaway: Find the -ation noun, strip it whole, add -er — and let je veux pull it into a sentence.

title: The Célébrer Trap
subtitle: Strip, don't trim — discrimination drills for the -ation engine

use_example.german: Je veux réserver, pas célébrater.
use_example.english: I want to reserve — not to 'celebrater'.

summary.takeaway: The -ation noun is the test and the vehicle: convert it, then strip it whole.

title: Je veux + Infinitive Gym
subtitle: Chain the converted verbs into real sentences

use_example.german: Tu veux organiser l'invitation ?
use_example.english: Do you want to organize the invitation?

summary.takeaway: Only the want-verb bends. The infinitive is parked freight — and every -ation noun is a new car.

title: The -ir & -re Verb Bridges
subtitle: finir (finish), choisir (choose), vendre (vendor), répondre (respond) — French's other two verb families

use_example.german: Je veux finir mon café et choisir un gâteau.
use_example.english: I want to finish my coffee and choose a cake.

summary.takeaway: English -ish verbs are French -ir verbs in disguise, and they chain after je veux just like -er verbs.

title: Ne...Pas: The Sandwich
subtitle: Negation wraps the verb — and pas is literally a footstep

use_example.german: Je ne le veux pas, merci.
use_example.english: I don't want it, thanks.

summary.takeaway: ne [verb] pas hugs the verb — pas is a refused footstep, and the pronoun lives inside the hug.

title: Pas Un Pas
subtitle: The footstep etymology gym: negation as refusing to move

use_example.german: Je n'y vais pas un pas.
use_example.english: I'm not going, not one step.

summary.takeaway: Negation is a refused noun with a history — and the sandwich always grips the conjugated verb, never the parked one.

title: Negation in the Wild
subtitle: Flip drills: statement → negative without moving anything else

use_example.german: Ce n'est pas possible — mais ce n'est pas grave.
use_example.english: It's not possible — but it's not serious.

summary.takeaway: The flip is two words around the verb. Even c'est un-fuses to be hugged.

title: être & Its Secrets
subtitle: c'est, je suis ('I follow'), tu es — the being-verbs as evidence

use_example.german: C'est très bon — je suis content.
use_example.english: It's very good — I'm happy.

summary.takeaway: est/is is the oldest cognate you own; suis means 'I follow'; c'est is the door when in doubt.

title: je suis: I Follow
subtitle: The sequence etymology, drilled into description sentences

use_example.german: Je suis grand, tu es petit.
use_example.english: I am tall, you are small.

summary.takeaway: je suis = I follow — and every description after être agrees with the person it paints.

title: C'est Gym
subtitle: The pointer verb: identification, questions, and la vie

use_example.german: Est-ce que c'est la vie ? — Oui, c'est la vie.
use_example.english: Is that life? — Yes, that's life.

summary.takeaway: c'est points, est-ce que asks — and neither disturbs the sentence underneath.

title: The -ité & -ance Bridges
subtitle: English -ity becomes -ité, -ance/-ence stays whole — and every single one takes la

use_example.german: L'université et la liberté sont très importantes.
use_example.english: The university and freedom are very important.

summary.takeaway: Four endings (-ion, -ité, -ance, -ence) hand you thousands of feminine nouns without a single flashcard.

title: The Feminine Squad
subtitle: -ion, -ité, -ance: convert 12 nouns and read their gender straight off the ending.

use_example.german: La patience est une grande qualité.
use_example.english: Patience is a great quality.

summary.takeaway: Glance at the suffix first: -ion, -ité, -ance, -ence = 100% feminine.

title: Liberté & Society Sentences
subtitle: La liberté est… — build sentences converting -ité and -ance nouns into the wild.

use_example.german: La qualité est très importante dans cette ville.
use_example.english: Quality is very important in this city.

summary.takeaway: Never leave an abstract noun bare in French: 'Freedom' is always La liberté.

title: The -ment & -able Twin Bridges
subtitle: Adverbs in -ment (exactement, naturellement) and adjectives in -able/-ible (possible, capable).

use_example.german: Finalement, c'est vraiment possible.
use_example.english: In the end, it's really possible.

summary.takeaway: English -ly is French feminine + -ment, and -able/-ible words cross unchanged.

title: Questions à la Française
subtitle: Three ladders of asking: rising voice, est-ce que, and inversion — plus cognate question words

use_example.german: Pourquoi est-ce que tu es ici ? — Parce que je veux te voir.
use_example.english: Why are you here? — Because I want to see you.

summary.takeaway: est-ce que is your universal question adapter: snap it after any question word and keep normal sentence order.

title: Est-ce que Drills
subtitle: 'Is it that': turn statements into questions without moving a single word.

use_example.german: Est-ce qu'on va au café maintenant ?
use_example.english: Are we going to the café now?

summary.takeaway: Est-ce que absorbs the inversion so your sentence never has to move.

title: Question-Word Twins
subtitle: où ↔ ubiquitous, pourquoi ↔ wherefore, quand, comment, combien — the cognate question words.

use_example.german: Quelle heure est-il et quand est-ce qu'on part ?
use_example.english: What time is it and when are we leaving?

summary.takeaway: où = ubiquitous, quel = quality, pourquoi = wherefore.

title: The -eur Bridge
subtitle: doctor → docteur, actor → acteur — and why la couleur and l'erreur rebel against masculine gender

use_example.german: Le professeur explique l'erreur.
use_example.english: The teacher explains the mistake.

summary.takeaway: British spelling 'colour' is a fossil of Old French — modern French moved on to -eur.

title: Couleur: The Famous Rebel
subtitle: la couleur, l'erreur, la peur, la chaleur: why abstract Latin -or nouns stayed feminine in French.

use_example.german: Quelle belle couleur sur cette fleur !
use_example.english: What a beautiful color on this flower!

summary.takeaway: People in -eur are le; qualities and sensations in -eur are la.

title: -eur Discrimination Drills
subtitle: Convert -or/-er nouns to -eur and decide le vs la using the agent vs quality rule.

use_example.german: C'est un grand honneur de voir le directeur.
use_example.english: It is a great honour to see the director.

summary.takeaway: Check un/une when l' hides the article: un acteur, un honneur, une erreur.

title: vous & tu
subtitle: The T–V politeness line: tu vs vous, the universal -ez ending, and social register

use_example.german: Bonjour, vous voulez un café, s'il vous plaît ?
use_example.english: Hello, would you like a coffee, please?

summary.takeaway: With vous, -ez (/e/) is your master key — and it sounds identical to the -er infinitive.

title: Merci & Bonjour Gym
subtitle: Greetings, thanks, s'il vous plaît — the politeness set in dialogue drills.

use_example.german: Bonjour ! Un thé, s'il vous plaît. — Merci !
use_example.english: Hello! A tea, please. — Thank you!

summary.takeaway: Always open with Bonjour before asking a question in France.

title: The vous Register
subtitle: When vous is required; vous voulez vs tu veux and the universal -ez ending.

use_example.german: Tu viens ? — Oui ! Et vous, vous venez avec nous ?
use_example.english: Are you coming? — Yes! And you all, are you coming with us?

summary.takeaway: One friend is tu; one stranger is vous; two of anybody is vous.

title: avoir & the H It Lost
subtitle: j'ai, tu as, il a, vous avez — plus the silent H doublets (hôtel/hospital, homme/human)

use_example.german: J'ai rendez-vous à l'hôtel dans une heure.
use_example.english: I have an appointment at the hotel in an hour.

summary.takeaway: French H is a silent ghost of Latin, and circumflex ˆ is the tombstone of a vanished S.

title: The H-Drop Doublets
subtitle: hôtel/hospital, homme/human, hiver/hibernate — French's silent H as an etymological fingerprint.

use_example.german: L'homme raconte une bonne histoire à l'hôtel.
use_example.english: The man tells a good story at the hotel.

summary.takeaway: To a French ear, Latin H is invisible — elide and link right through it.

title: J'ai Gym
subtitle: J'ai un gâteau, j'ai trente ans — have-sentences including age as possession.

use_example.german: J'ai trente ans et j'ai deux frères.
use_example.english: I am thirty years old and I have two brothers.

summary.takeaway: J'ai flips to Je n'ai pas de in the negative.

title: Liaison & Silent Consonants: CaReFuL
subtitle: Why final consonants go silent except C, R, F, L — and wake up before a vowel in liaison (vous avez, les amis).

use_example.german: Vous avez un bon ami à l'hôtel.
use_example.english: You have a good friend at the hotel.

summary.takeaway: Final consonants sleep unless they are CaReFuL — or unless the next word's vowel wakes them up.

title: Adjectives & the Silent -s
subtitle: Feminine -e wakes the sleeping final consonant (grand → grande), plural -s stays silent, and colors follow the noun

use_example.german: Un café noir à la table rouge.
use_example.english: A black coffee at the red table.

summary.takeaway: Feminine -e wakes the sleeping final consonant, and colors always paint the noun from behind.

title: The e and the s
subtitle: Feminine -e wakes the sleeping final consonant (grand → grande); plural -s stays silent.

use_example.german: Les jardins sont verts et les maisons sont blanches.
use_example.english: The gardens are green and the houses are white.

summary.takeaway: Four written forms (grand, grands, grande, grandes), only two spoken sounds (/ɡʁɑ̃/ and /ɡʁɑ̃d/).

title: Color & Size Gym
subtitle: Le jardin vert, la maison blanche — adjective placement after the noun.

use_example.german: Elle habite dans une petite maison jaune.
use_example.english: She lives in a small yellow house.

summary.takeaway: Size in front, color in back: un petit café noir.

title: BAGS: Adjectives Before the Noun
subtitle: Beauty, Age, Goodness, Size (beau, jeune, bon, petit, grand, nouveau) — the high-frequency rebels that step in front.

use_example.german: Un petit café noir dans un bel hôtel.
use_example.english: A small black coffee in a beautiful hotel.

summary.takeaway: BAGS steps in front, colors stay in back — and beau/nouveau/vieux wear -l before a masculine vowel.

title: The Near Future
subtitle: aller + infinitive: je vais visiter, tu vas voir, on va partir — and aller is English 'amble'

use_example.german: On va voir un film ce soir.
use_example.english: We're going to see a film tonight.

summary.takeaway: aller + bare infinitive gives you the entire future tense today — with zero new endings to memorize.

title: Amble & Go
subtitle: The ambulāre etymology; vais, vas, va, allons, allez in motion drills.

use_example.german: Où est-ce que vous allez ? — Nous allons à la gare.
use_example.english: Where are you going? — We are going to the station.

summary.takeaway: je vais (/vɛ/), tu vas (/va/), il/on va (/va/), nous allons, vous allez.

title: Future Gym
subtitle: Near-future sentences chaining je vais / tu vas / on va with converted verbs.

use_example.german: Ce soir, on va préparer un bon dîner et célébrer.
use_example.english: Tonight, we're going to prepare a good dinner and celebrate.

summary.takeaway: Conjugate aller, park the infinitive, and hug aller with ne...pas when negating.

title: à, de, chez
subtitle: The two master prepositions (à and de), their mandatory fusions (au, du, des), and chez ('at the home/place of')

use_example.german: On va chez Marie ou au restaurant ?
use_example.english: Are we going to Marie's place or to the restaurant?

summary.takeaway: Buildings take au / à la; people take chez — and *à le / *de le never exist.

title: au & du Fusions
subtitle: à + le = au, de + le = du, de + les = des: mandatory contractions as word-glue.

use_example.german: Je sors de l'hôtel et je vais au café en face de la gare.
use_example.english: I leave the hotel and go to the café across from the station.

summary.takeaway: Vowel → à l' / de l'; Feminine → à la / de la; Masculine → au / du.

title: Chez, the House Word
subtitle: chez Marie, chez le docteur, chez moi — the Latin casa preposition with no English twin.

use_example.german: Tu viens chez moi ou on va chez toi ?
use_example.english: Are you coming to my place or are we going to yours?

summary.takeaway: Places take au / à la; people take chez.

title: The Partitive: du, de la & Negative de
subtitle: Why French says 'some bread' (du pain, de la soupe) and collapses it to bare de after negation (pas de pain).

use_example.german: Je prends du pain et de la soupe, mais je ne prends pas de vin.
use_example.english: I'm having bread and soup, but I'm not having wine.

summary.takeaway: Use du / de la / de l' / des for 'some', and collapse to bare de after pas.

title: Possessives Agree with the Thing
subtitle: mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes, son/sa/ses — why 'son frère' means both 'his brother' and 'her brother'

use_example.german: Paul cherche sa sœur et Marie cherche son frère.
use_example.english: Paul is looking for his sister and Marie is looking for her brother.

summary.takeaway: Possessives look right (at the noun owned), never left (at the owner).

title: The Trap Named
subtitle: mon frère / ma sœur, son frère ('his OR her brother'), and mon before feminine vowels (mon opinion).

use_example.german: C'est mon idée, mon opinion et mon histoire.
use_example.english: It is my idea, my opinion, and my story.

summary.takeaway: Ignore the owner's gender, and use mon/ton/son before every vowel.

title: Famille Gym
subtitle: Drills across père, mère, frère, sœur, famille with mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes, son/sa/ses.

use_example.german: Notre famille aime beaucoup vos amis.
use_example.english: Our family likes your friends a lot.

summary.takeaway: mon/ton/son split m/f/pl; notre/votre/leur only split singular vs. plural.

title: Demonstratives & Stressed Pronouns
subtitle: Pointing with ce/cet/cette/ces and standing alone after prepositions with moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous.

use_example.german: Cet hôtel est très beau — tu viens avec moi ?
use_example.english: This hotel is very beautiful — are you coming with me?

summary.takeaway: ce becomes cet before a masculine vowel, and prepositions always take moi, toi, lui, elle.

title: Numbers & the Four-Twenties
subtitle: Counting 1–100, vigesimal quatre-vingts ('four score'), and expressing age as possession with avoir

use_example.german: Mon père a soixante ans et j'ai trente ans.
use_example.english: My father is sixty and I am thirty.

summary.takeaway: 80 is four-twenties (quatre-vingts), and you always 'have' your years (j'ai X ans).

title: Counting Cognates Gym
subtitle: un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix, vingt — Latin roots in everyday counting.

use_example.german: J'attends depuis cinq minutes.
use_example.english: I've been waiting for five minutes.

summary.takeaway: Numbers 1–20 are Latin cognates you already own in English.

title: Four Score & Seven
subtitle: soixante-dix (60+10), quatre-vingts (4×20), and expressing age with avoir (j'ai trente ans).

use_example.german: Ma grand-mère a quatre-vingts ans.
use_example.english: My grandmother is eighty years old.

summary.takeaway: 70 is sixty-ten, 80 is four-twenties, and 100 is bare cent.

title: Days, Months & Dates
subtitle: The planetary weekdays (lundi to dimanche), months with en, dates with le, and aujourd'hui

use_example.german: Le dimanche, je reste chez moi.
use_example.english: On Sundays, I stay at home.

summary.takeaway: Weekdays take no 'on' (lundi = on Monday, le lundi = every Monday), and months take en.

title: The Sky Calendar
subtitle: lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche — the Roman planetary week.

use_example.german: On se voit mercredi ou jeudi ?
use_example.english: Shall we see each other Wednesday or Thursday?

summary.takeaway: Five Roman gods + Sabbath + Lord's Day = the French week.

title: En janvier Gym
subtitle: Months with en (en janvier, en juillet), dates with le, and aujourd'hui / demain / hier.

use_example.german: Mon frère est né en juillet.
use_example.english: My brother was born in July.

summary.takeaway: en + month ('en juillet'); le + number + month ('le quatorze juillet').

title: The -é Past
subtitle: The passé composé with avoir: j'ai mangé, tu as parlé — where -é is English -ed

use_example.german: Hier, j'ai parlé avec mon ami et j'ai compris.
use_example.english: Yesterday, I spoke with my friend and I understood.

summary.takeaway: One two-word tense (avoir + participle) does the job of both 'I did' and 'I have done'.

title: Participle Twins
subtitle: mangé, décidé, parlé, trouvé, donné, aimé, fini, compris, pris, vu — the -é/-i/-u participle system.

use_example.german: J'ai déjà pris mon billet et j'ai fait ma valise.
use_example.english: I already got my ticket and packed my suitcase.

summary.takeaway: Short adverbs like déjà sit between avoir and the participle: J'ai déjà vu.

title: Hier j'ai… Story Drills
subtitle: Narrate a past day in passé composé sentences with avoir.

use_example.german: Hier, j'ai réservé une table et nous avons célébré.
use_example.english: Yesterday, I reserved a table and we celebrated.

summary.takeaway: In speech, je vais /vizite/ and j'ai /vizite/ differ only by vais vs. ai; in writing, vais takes -er and ai takes -é.

title: Motion Takes être
subtitle: je suis allé(e), elle est venue, il est parti — the motion verbs that take être in the past and agree like adjectives

use_example.german: Je suis allé à la gare et elle est venue avec moi.
use_example.english: I went to the station and she came with me.

summary.takeaway: Whole-body motion and doorway verbs take être ('I am gone'), and their participle agrees with the traveller.

title: The être House
subtitle: allé, arrivé, venu, parti, sorti, monté, descendu, resté, tombé, né — the doorway-and-motion verb house.

use_example.german: Il est entré, il est resté cinq minutes, et il est reparti.
use_example.english: He came in, stayed five minutes, and left again.

summary.takeaway: Remember the être house in opposite pairs: go/come, arrive/leave, enter/exit, up/down.

title: Agreement Drills
subtitle: allée, allés, allées: why participles wear gender and plural agreements only inside the être house.

use_example.german: Elle est sortie, mais elle a oublié son parapluie.
use_example.english: She went out, but she forgot her umbrella.

summary.takeaway: être participles agree with the subject (Elle est allée); avoir participles do not (Elle a mangé).

title: The Storytelling Past
subtitle: The imparfait camera lens: c'était, j'avais, j'habitais, je voulais — ongoing background vs. completed event

use_example.german: C'était magnifique quand nous habitions là.
use_example.english: It was wonderful when we used to live there.

summary.takeaway: Passé composé is the event dot; imparfait (-ais/-ait) is the background canvas — and c'était is its king.

title: Was & Was-Ing
subtitle: The -ais/-ait imparfait camera lens: c'était, il y avait, j'avais, je voulais.

use_example.german: C'était une belle soirée et il y avait un bon concert.
use_example.english: It was a lovely evening and there was a good concert.

summary.takeaway: c'est → c'était ('it was'); il y a → il y avait ('there was/were').

title: Imparfait vs Composé
subtitle: Background canvas (imparfait) interrupted by the event dot (passé composé).

use_example.german: Il faisait beau quand nous sommes sortis.
use_example.english: The weather was nice when we went out.

summary.takeaway: Background state = Imparfait (-ais/-ait); Foreground action = Passé composé.

title: depuis & the Perfect Split
subtitle: J'habite ici depuis trois ans — why French uses the present tense where English says 'I have lived here for three years'

use_example.german: Je suis ici depuis une heure.
use_example.english: I've been here for an hour.

summary.takeaway: If it is still happening right now, French refuses the past tense: Present + depuis.

title: The Trap Lesson
subtitle: depuis + present tense: why ongoing actions stay in the present in French.

use_example.german: Nous sommes amis depuis vingt ans.
use_example.english: We have been friends for twenty years.

summary.takeaway: Ongoing action = Present tense + depuis (for both 'for' and 'since').

title: Since & For Gym
subtitle: depuis quand ? — building duration sentences across work, study, and residence.

use_example.german: Tu apprends le français depuis quand ? — Depuis ce matin !
use_example.english: How long have you been learning French? — Since this morning!

summary.takeaway: 'How long have you...?' is Present Tense + depuis quand ?

title: Plus, Moins, aussi
subtitle: Comparing with plus… que, moins… que, aussi… que — and the twin suppletions bon → meilleur and mauvais → pire

use_example.german: Le train est plus rapide et moins cher que la voiture.
use_example.english: The train is faster and cheaper than the car.

summary.takeaway: Every comparison closes with que — and 'better' is always meilleur.

title: The Twin Suppletions
subtitle: bon → meilleur (ameliorate) and mauvais → pire (pejorative): frozen Latin comparatives.

use_example.german: C'est la meilleure idée de la journée.
use_example.english: It's the best idea of the day.

summary.takeaway: Add le/la/les to any comparative to make the superlative: meilleur → le meilleur ('the best').

title: Comparison Gym
subtitle: plus… que, moins… que, aussi… que across cities, food, and ideas.

use_example.german: Ce bistro est moins cher et aussi bon que le restaurant.
use_example.english: This bistro is cheaper and just as good as the restaurant.

summary.takeaway: 'as... as' is aussi... que (never comme), and the adjective agrees with the first noun.

title: en & y
subtitle: j'en veux ('I want some / of it') and j'y vais ('I'm going there') — the two adverbial pronouns that walk left

use_example.german: Tu vas à la boulangerie ? — Oui, j'y vais et j'en prends deux.
use_example.english: Are you going to the bakery? — Yes, I'm going there and getting two of them.

summary.takeaway: à + place becomes y ('there'); de + thing/quantity becomes en ('of it').

title: en: Of It
subtitle: en replaces de + noun and partitives: Tu veux du café ? — Oui, j'en veux.

use_example.german: Tu as du pain ? — Oui, j'en ai beaucoup.
use_example.english: Do you have bread? — Yes, I have a lot of it.

summary.takeaway: Whenever a number or quantity stands without its noun, en must stand before the verb (J'en ai deux).

title: y: There
subtitle: y replaces à/dans/chez + place: Tu vas à Paris ? — Oui, j'y vais.

use_example.german: C'est une belle ville — je voudrais y habiter.
use_example.english: It's a beautiful city — I would like to live there.

summary.takeaway: Single verb: J'y vais; Infinitive chain: Je veux y aller.

title: Pronouns Walk Left
subtitle: me, te, le, la, nous, vous, lui, leur — direct and indirect object pronouns walking left of the verb

use_example.german: Je le vois et je lui parle.
use_example.english: I see him and I speak to him/her.

summary.takeaway: le/la is direct ('him/her'); lui is indirect ('to him / to her') — and both walk left of the verb.

title: The Full Left-Walk
subtitle: je te vois, tu me comprends, il nous écoute — direct object pronouns walking before the verb.

use_example.german: Je t'attends ici et je vais t'aider.
use_example.english: I'm waiting for you here and I'm going to help you.

summary.takeaway: Single verb: Je te vois; Infinitive chain: Je veux te voir.

title: lui & leur
subtitle: je lui parle ('I speak to him OR to her'), je leur donne — gender-neutral indirect objects.

use_example.german: Ma mère m'appelle — je vais lui répondre.
use_example.english: My mother is calling me — I'm going to answer her.

summary.takeaway: parler, répondre, demander, donner all take à → use lui (him/her) and leur (them).

title: The Double-Pronoun Highway
subtitle: Stacking two pronouns before the verb in strict order: me le, le lui, and y/en last.

use_example.german: Tu veux le livre ? — Oui, tu me le donnes ?
use_example.english: Do you want the book? — Yes, will you give it to me?

summary.takeaway: me/te/nous/vous go before le/la/les; le/la/les go before lui/leur; and y/en ride at the back.

title: Reflexives & la Routine
subtitle: se lever, se laver, s'habiller, se coucher — when the subject and the left-walking pronoun are the same person

use_example.german: Je me lève à sept heures et je m'habille.
use_example.english: I get up at seven o'clock and get dressed.

summary.takeaway: Reflexives are just left-walking pronouns pointing back at the subject — and they adapt to the speaker even before an infinitive.

title: I Call Myself
subtitle: je m'appelle, tu t'appelles, on se voit — reflexive pronouns in everyday interaction.

use_example.german: On s'appelle demain et on se voit samedi !
use_example.english: We'll call each other tomorrow and see each other Saturday!

summary.takeaway: With on/nous/vous, reflexive pronouns also mean 'each other' (On se voit !).

title: The Morning Round
subtitle: se lever, se laver, s'habiller, se coucher — chaining daily routine verbs.

use_example.german: Ce matin, je me suis levé tôt et je me suis habillé.
use_example.english: This morning, I got up early and got dressed.

summary.takeaway: All reflexives take être in the past (Je me suis levé), and body parts take le/la/les (Je me lave les mains).

title: il y a
subtitle: 'It has there' = there is / there are — and with a time span, 'ago' (il y a trois ans)

use_example.german: Il y a deux ans, il y avait un petit café ici.
use_example.english: Two years ago, there was a small café here.

summary.takeaway: il + y + a ('it there has') means 'there is/are' in space and 'ago' in time.

title: It Has There
subtitle: il y a un café ('there is a café') vs il y a trois ans ('three years ago').

use_example.german: Il y a dix ans, j'habitais à Lyon.
use_example.english: Ten years ago, I used to live in Lyon.

summary.takeaway: Before a time span in the past, il y a means 'ago'.

title: il y a Gym
subtitle: Negating and questioning existence: il n'y a pas de…, est-ce qu'il y a…?

use_example.german: Il n'y a pas de problème, il y en a beaucoup.
use_example.english: There's no problem, there's plenty of it.

summary.takeaway: Il y a → Il n'y a pas de (none) → Il y en a (there is some).

title: The Would-World
subtitle: je voudrais, tu pourrais, je ferais — the conditional politeness escalator and the -ai future tense

use_example.german: Je voudrais vous demander une information.
use_example.english: I would like to ask you for a piece of information.

summary.takeaway: Future stem (/ʁ/) + -ai is 'will'; Future stem (/ʁ/) + -ais is 'would'.

title: Je voudrais
subtitle: vouloir, pouvoir, faire in the conditional (je voudrais, tu pourrais, je ferais).

use_example.german: Bonjour, je voudrais deux billets pour Lyon, s'il vous plaît.
use_example.english: Hello, I would like two tickets to Lyon, please.

summary.takeaway: Swap je veux for je voudrais whenever you order or ask a favor.

title: The -ai Future
subtitle: Infinitive + avoir's present endings: je parlerai, tu visiteras, on ira.

use_example.german: Tu verras, ce sera une belle aventure !
use_example.english: You'll see, it will be a great adventure!

summary.takeaway: Every future stem ends in -r-; add -ai/-as/-a for 'will' and -ais/-ait for 'would'.

title: il faut
subtitle: 'It is needed' — subjectless necessity (il faut partir) and the subjunctive bridge (il faut que tu sois là)

use_example.german: Il faut partir maintenant — il me faut mon manteau.
use_example.english: We have to leave now — I need my coat.

summary.takeaway: il faut never changes its subject; pair it with an infinitive for general necessity or que + subjunctive for a specific person.

title: It Is Needed
subtitle: il faut + infinitive (il faut partir, il faut voir) and il me faut + noun.

use_example.german: Qu'est-ce qu'il te faut ? — Il me faut mon billet.
use_example.english: What do you need? — I need my ticket.

summary.takeaway: Il faut + verb = 'must [verb]'; Il me faut + noun = 'I need [noun]'.

title: The Subjunctive Door
subtitle: il faut que tu sois là, je veux que tu viennes — when necessity or desire crosses between two subjects.

use_example.german: Il est tard, il faut que j'y aille !
use_example.english: It's late, I've got to get going!

summary.takeaway: English 'I want you to [verb]' is ALWAYS French 'Je veux que tu [subjunctive]'.

title: Savoir vs Connaître
subtitle: Knowing facts and skills (je sais nager) vs being familiar with people and places (je connais Paris).

use_example.german: Je connais bien cette ville, donc je sais où aller.
use_example.english: I know this city well, so I know where to go.

summary.takeaway: connaître + Noun (people/places); savoir + Clause or Bare Infinitive (facts/skills).

title: qui & que
subtitle: Relative pronouns qui (subject), que (object), and dont ('of which') — welding two sentences into one

use_example.german: La ville où j'habite et le café que j'aime.
use_example.english: The city where I live and the café that I love.

summary.takeaway: qui + verb, que + subject, dont for de — and never leave 'that' out.

title: The Man That Knows
subtitle: qui for the subject after the gap (l'homme qui parle), que for the object (le café que je veux).

use_example.german: Le train qui part maintenant est le train que je voulais prendre.
use_example.english: The train that is leaving now is the train that I wanted to take.

summary.takeaway: Verb after the gap → qui (never elides); Subject after the gap → que / qu' (never omitted).

title: Que Everywhere
subtitle: je pense que, je sais que, c'est… que — que as the master clause connector.

use_example.german: Je sais qu'il est tard, mais je pense que c'est possible.
use_example.english: I know it's late, but I think it's possible.

summary.takeaway: English drops 'that'; French NEVER drops que.

title: Verb Dynasties: venir, tenir & prendre Matrices
subtitle: Prefix × root matrices: re-/de-/ob-/main-/com-/ap- across venir, tenir, and prendre.

use_example.german: J'apprends vite et je vais revenir demain.
use_example.english: I learn quickly and I'm going to come back tomorrow.

summary.takeaway: Learn three roots (venir, tenir, prendre) and six prefixes, and two dozen verbs conjugate themselves.

title: The French Mind
subtitle: avoir faim, avoir soif, avoir raison, avoir besoin de — feelings as possessions and idioms as thought

use_example.german: Tu as raison, j'ai besoin de manger parce que j'ai faim.
use_example.english: You're right, I need to eat because I'm hungry.

summary.takeaway: In French, you don't 'be' hungry, thirsty, afraid, or right — you 'have' hunger, thirst, fear, and reason.

title: Have-Hunger & Co
subtitle: Feelings as possessions with avoir: avoir faim, soif, peur, raison, besoin de.

use_example.german: J'ai froid et j'ai faim — allons au bistro !
use_example.english: I'm cold and I'm hungry — let's go to the bistro!

summary.takeaway: People 'have' hunger, thirst, cold, heat, fear, and reason with avoir.

title: The Register Ladder Recap
subtitle: Walking the 9 conversion bridges from English formal register into everyday French.

use_example.german: Finalement, l'organisation a confirmé la possibilité.
use_example.english: Finally, the organization confirmed the possibility.

summary.takeaway: Nine suffix bridges turn your English vocabulary into a live French lexicon.

title: Spoken French Shortcuts
subtitle: on = nous, dropped ne, t'as / y'a — decoding fast street French without losing the structure.

use_example.german: On va au bistro ? — Oui, on y va !
use_example.english: Shall we go to the bistro? — Yes, let's go!

summary.takeaway: In spoken French, 'we' is on (with the il/elle verb), and ne disappears while pas does the work.

title: Capstone: Le Pont Reading
subtitle: Walking across Le Pont in Paris — every conversion bridge, tense frame, and left-walking pronoun in one living story

use_example.german: Je comprends maintenant le français que j'avais déjà dans la tête.
use_example.english: I now understand the French that I already had inside my head.

summary.takeaway: You didn't memorize a foreign language from scratch — you unlocked the French half of your own English.

title: A Day in Paris: Reading
subtitle: The capstone narrative in Paris synthesizing all 9 conversion bridges and tense frames.

use_example.german: Quand je suis sorti de la gare, j'ai vu que la ville était magnifique.
use_example.english: When I walked out of the station, I saw that the city was magnificent.

summary.takeaway: Real stories weave Passé composé (events), Imparfait (scene), and Present + depuis (ongoing truths).

title: Trap Watch: False Friends in the Wild
subtitle: High-frequency false friends (actuellement, librairie, attendre, raisin, journée, location) in context.

use_example.german: Merci beaucoup et bonne journée !
use_example.english: Thank you very much and have a great day!

summary.takeaway: la journée = the day; le raisin = fresh grape; la location = rental; formidable = wonderful.

title: The Whole-Trail Review Game
subtitle: Mixed-mode synthesis across all 30 topics of Le Pont.

use_example.german: Je sais maintenant que je peux parler français.
use_example.english: I know now that I can speak French.

summary.takeaway: Every complex French sentence is built from simple, transparent pieces you now own.

title: Bonjour & Merci
subtitle: Greetings, thanks, and ça va — the politeness set in dialogue

use_example.german: Bonjour ! Ça va ? — Ça va, merci.
use_example.english: Hello! How's it going? — Fine, thanks.

summary.takeaway: Idioms are items, not formulas — and vous is the pronoun you can't be fired for.

title: The Alphabet & Je m'appelle
subtitle: Spelling your name: w is double-v, y is i-grec

use_example.german: Je m'appelle Alex. Et vous ?
use_example.english: My name is Alex. And you?

summary.takeaway: Introductions are reflexive and elided — the same pronoun machinery, pointed at yourself.

title: Think the N
subtitle: The four nasal vowels: on, en, an, in — the sound of not arriving

use_example.german: Le pain est bon, on y va.
use_example.english: The bread is good — shall we?

summary.takeaway: The N is a direction, not a destination. Unfinished is correct.

title: Actuellement, Librairie & Co.
subtitle: The trap deck in the wild: same word, different soul

use_example.german: Je demande mon chemin à la librairie.
use_example.english: I ask for directions at the bookshop.

summary.takeaway: Spelling converts reliably; meaning converts mostly. The Review Hub keeps the liars in rotation.

title: Tutoyer & Vouvoyer
subtitle: Choosing tu vs vous as social verbs, and how on ('one/the man') became spoken French's everyday 'we'.

use_example.german: Au travail, on se tutoie tous.
use_example.english: At work, we all use 'tu' with each other.

summary.takeaway: Wait for 'On se tutoie ?' to switch from vous to tu — and use on for everyday 'we'.

title: Lieu & Direction: ici, là, tout droit
subtitle: Navigating streets: tout droit, à gauche, à droite, où est la gare ?

use_example.german: Pardon, la gare ? — C'est tout droit, puis à gauche.
use_example.english: Excuse me, the station? — It's straight ahead, then on the left.

summary.takeaway: Straight ahead = tout droit; left = à gauche; right = à droite.

title: C'est combien ?
subtitle: Asking prices, ordering with numbers 1–100, and l'addition at the bistro.

use_example.german: Bonjour, c'est combien pour ce livre ? — Ça fait dix euros.
use_example.english: Hello, how much is it for this book? — That comes to ten euros.

summary.takeaway: How much = C'est combien ?; Total = Ça fait X euros; Restaurant check = L'addition.

title: Je n'ai pas mangé
subtitle: The sandwich wraps the auxiliary (je n'ai pas compris, tu n'as pas vu) and déjà slots inside.

use_example.german: Je n'ai jamais vu ce film, mais j'ai déjà lu le livre.
use_example.english: I've never seen this movie, but I've already read the book.

summary.takeaway: In the past tense, pas, jamais, rien, and déjà always sit between the auxiliary and the participle.

title: De matin à soir
subtitle: Chaining reflexives (se lever, se laver, s'habiller, se coucher) across a full day.

use_example.german: La semaine, je me lève tôt, mais le dimanche je me repose.
use_example.english: During the week I get up early, but on Sundays I rest.

summary.takeaway: ne...pas hugs the reflexive pronoun and verb together: Je ne me lève pas.

title: Dont & Où
subtitle: dont ('of which / whose') for de-verbs and où as relative 'where/when'.

use_example.german: Le jour où je suis arrivé dans la ville dont tu parles.
use_example.english: The day when I arrived in the city you're talking about.

summary.takeaway: de-verb → dont; place or 'the day when' → où.

title: Tout le conditionnel
subtitle: Building any conditional from the future stem + imparfait ending (-ais, -ait).

use_example.german: Si j'habitais à Paris, j'irais au musée tous les dimanches.
use_example.english: If I lived in Paris, I would go to the museum every Sunday.

summary.takeaway: After si ('if') use the imparfait (Si j'avais); in the result use the conditional (j'irais).

title: Dormant Consonants Wake Up
subtitle: S→/z/ (vous avez, les amis), T→/t/ (c'est un), N→/n/ (un ami) — reading connected French speech.

use_example.german: On arrive à huit heures avec nos amis.
use_example.english: We arrive at eight o'clock with our friends.

summary.takeaway: S/X → /z/, T/D → /t/, N → /n/, and 'et' never links.

title: H muet vs H aspiré
subtitle: Why l'hôtel and l'homme elide and link, while le héros refuses elision.

use_example.german: C'est le héros de l'histoire.
use_example.english: He is the hero of the story.

summary.takeaway: Both H's are silent; Latin H muet elides (l'histoire), while H aspiré stands apart (le héros).

title: Le Pain, Le Fromage, Le Vin & L'Eau
subtitle: The French table staples with definite vs partitive articles (le pain vs du pain).

use_example.german: J'adore le fromage français — j'en prends toujours avec du pain.
use_example.english: I love French cheese — I always have some with bread.

summary.takeaway: Liking in general = le / la / l'; Eating or ordering some = du / de la / de l'.

title: Commander au Bistro
subtitle: Taking a table, ordering with je prends / je voudrais, and asking for l'addition.

use_example.german: Qu'est-ce que tu prends ? — Je prends un café et un croissant.
use_example.english: What are you having? — I'll have a coffee and a croissant.

summary.takeaway: To order food or drink, English 'I'll have' is always French Je prends ('I take').

title: Le Train, Le Billet & La Gare
subtitle: Navigating the SNCF: le train, le billet, la gare, réservations, and platforms.

use_example.german: Je vais à la gare parce que je prends le train de midi.
use_example.english: I'm going to the station because I'm taking the noon train.

summary.takeaway: You 'take' both coffee and trains with prendre: Je prends un café, je prends le train.

title: Départ, Arrivée & Aller-Retour
subtitle: Combining aller, partir, arriver, and prendre for real travel scenarios.

use_example.german: Un aller-retour pour Bordeaux, s'il vous plaît.
use_example.english: A round-trip ticket to Bordeaux, please.

summary.takeaway: One-way = un aller simple; Round-trip = un aller-retour; Ticket destination = pour [City].

title: Docteur, Professeur & Acteur
subtitle: Why French drops 'a/an' before professions after être: Je suis professeur, il est docteur.

use_example.german: Mon père est directeur et ma sœur est professeure.
use_example.english: My father is a director and my sister is a teacher.

summary.takeaway: After je suis / il est, drop 'a/an' before a bare profession (Je suis professeur); with an adjective, use C'est un bon professeur.

title: La Musique, Le Cinéma & Le Livre
subtitle: Talking about arts, cinema, books, and passions with aimer and préférer.

use_example.german: J'adore la musique, mais ce soir je préfère lire un bon livre.
use_example.english: I love music, but tonight I prefer to read a good book.

summary.takeaway: After aimer/adorer/préférer, always keep le, la, l', les (J'aime la musique).

title: La Tête, La Main & Le Cœur
subtitle: Expressing aches with avoir mal à la tête and definite articles with body parts.

use_example.german: Je ne peux pas venir parce que j'ai mal à la tête.
use_example.english: I can't come because I have a headache.

summary.takeaway: Headache = J'ai mal à la tête (never *ma tête).

title: Le Manteau & La Robe
subtitle: Clothing doublets (manteau/mantle, robe/wardrobe) and adjective placement with colors.

use_example.german: Il fait froid, donc je porte mon grand manteau bleu.
use_example.english: It's cold, so I'm wearing my big blue coat.

summary.takeaway: Old French -el became modern French -eau (mantle → manteau, castle → château).
